title: A Podcast on Adab During Online Disagreements
script: Host: [thoughtful] Welcome back. Today's guest manages social media for a small nonprofit, and he wants to discuss adab in online disagreements. Thanks for joining me, Fikri.
Guest: Thanks for having me. This topic became personal after a comment section incident I still think about occasionally.
Host: [carefully] What happened, if you don't mind sharing it?
Guest: Someone left a harsh comment criticizing our organization's approach, and honestly, my first instinct was to respond defensively, immediately, in public.
Host: [reflective] What stopped you from doing that?
Guest: I typed a reply, read it back, and realized it was written entirely to win an argument rather than to actually address his concern.
Host: [honestly] So what did you do instead?
Guest: I waited an hour, then messaged him privately, thanking him for caring enough about the issue to comment at all.
Host: [seriously] Even though his comment had been harsh toward your organization?
Guest: Especially because it was harsh. People rarely comment harshly about things they don't care about, in my experience.
Host: [gently] Did that private message change the tone of the conversation?
Guest: Completely. He apologized for his tone, explained his actual concern calmly, and we ended up improving one of our programs because of it.
Host: [encouraging] Do you think adab online is different from adab in person, given how public everything becomes?
Guest: Slightly, yes, because online arguments have an audience, which tempts people toward performing rather than genuinely resolving anything.
Host: [sincere] What advice would you give someone tempted to respond angrily to a public comment?

Guest: Pause before typing, ask whether your reply is meant to inform or to humiliate, and use the channel that fits the risk: private dialogue for suitable matters; visible correction for public misinformation; and formal reporting for threats, harassment, safeguarding, fraud, or unlawful content.
Host: [thoughtful] That last point feels important. Public correction can feel like punishment, even when the facts are entirely correct.
Guest: Exactly. Being right shouldn't require someone else's public embarrassment, especially when a private message could achieve the same result gently.
Host: [carefully] Wonderful advice, Fikri. Thank you for sharing something so honest with our listeners today.
Guest: Thank you for having me. I hope it helps someone pause before hitting send next time.
